unit.title: Perform internal and external customer service

summary: This unit is about serving everyone who depends on your welding team's work: the clients who buy from the shop (external customers) and the people inside the business who take your work further (internal customers). You will learn to find out and confirm exactly what a client needs, advise on materials and finishes in plain words, give clear quotations and dates you can keep, refuse unsafe requests without losing the client, handle complaints and hand over work well, and set and measure service standards inside the shop.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **customer service** in a fabrication business: knowing who your customers are, finding out what they need, advising them, pricing and promising, keeping them informed, dealing with complaints, handing over the work and looking after them afterwards.

At Level 3 you are often the person the client meets. You visit the site, measure, explain the choices, give the date and take the angry phone call. Inside the shop you lead a team whose work feeds the painters, the inspector, the stores and the office. A well-made gate can still lose the shop a client if it is late, if nobody calls back, or if the yard is left full of rod stubs. Good welding and good service go together.

**Who it is for:** Welding Level 3 trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and welders who lead a team or deal with clients. The examples come from fabrication, but the same skills serve any trade.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in a fabrication shop
rows: Know your customers

Name the external customers (home owners, businesses, hotels, schools, farmers, contractors) and the internal customers (fitters, painting bay, inspector, stores, office, driver), and say what each needs from the welding team.
Find out and confirm needs
Ask good questions, listen, visit and measure the site yourself, and confirm the needs in writing with a sketch before you quote.
Advise clients
Explain material, finish and design choices in plain words, with the reasons and the cost of each, so the client can choose.
Give clear prices and dates
Write a quotation that shows the work, what is not included, the price in J$, GCT at the current rate, the deposit, the lead time and the warranty.
Manage expectations
Give dates you can meet, tell the client early about any delay, and agree changes in writing before you make them.
Handle unsafe or unwise requests
Explain the danger, refuse politely and firmly, and offer a safe way to meet the need.
Deal with complaints
Listen, apologise, record, inspect, put it right fairly, follow up, and fix the cause in the shop.
Hand over and look after the client
Check the work and the site, show the client how to use and care for the item, hand over the papers and call back afterwards.
Serve the team inside the shop
Pass on work that is clean, checked, labelled and on time; give clear information; agree and measure service standards.
Act honestly and keep confidences
Sign only for work you did, keep clients' details and security drawings private, and use the shop's equipment only for the shop's work.

ul: A **multiple-choice paper** on customers, needs, advice, prices, dates, complaints, handover, unsafe requests and service standards. Some questions ask you to work out a deposit or a percentage.

A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms (internal customer, deposit, warranty, delivery note, job card, lead time, marine environment) and simple sums; and longer answers in full sentences, for example on handling a complaint or advising a client on finishes.

**Practical tasks** done as a group: a role play of a site visit, a measured sketch and a written quotation for a gate; and handling a complaint about a faulty frame, inspecting it, writing the reply and agreeing internal service standards.

blocks.note: In the role plays the assessor watches how you deal with the client, not only the paperwork: open questions, real listening, plain words, checking that the client understood, and staying polite when the client is difficult. Every member must speak to the client and sign the part they prepared.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **customer** is anyone who depends on your work. **External customers** are outside the business and buy its goods or services. **Internal customers** work in the same business and need something from your team to do their own job: your finished frames, your cutting list, your job card.

head: External customer
What they usually need from the shop
rows: Home owner or walk-in client
The right size, a good finish, a fair price, the date kept, a clean yard, and plain explanations
Hotel, guest house or restaurant
Work that suits a coastal setting and guests nearby; work done at agreed times; reliable after-sales service
School, church or community group
Safe design for children, older people and wheelchair users; clear prices for a committee or board to approve
Farmer or small business
Strong, practical work done quickly so the business is not held up
Contractor or builder
Work that fits the drawings and the site programme, delivered when agreed, with the right paperwork

blocks.p: Work passes through many hands before the client sees it. Each step is the internal customer of the step before it.

flow: Enquiry taken by the office or the team leader
Site visit, measurements and quotation
Order and deposit; job card raised
Stores issue steel and consumables
Cutting and fitting
Welding
Inspection (quality control)
Painting, or sending out to the galvaniser
Delivery and fitting
Handover, invoice and after-sales

blocks.p: A fault or delay anywhere in the chain reaches the client in the end. Frames passed on with spatter and sharp edges mean extra grinding in the painting bay, a later finish and a poorer coat of paint, which rusts sooner. **Good internal service makes good external service possible.**

head: Internal customer
What they need from the welding team
How the team serves them well
rows: Fitters and cutting team
Clear cutting lists and drawings, checked and on time
Check the list against the drawing and its revision before you hand it over; never give sizes from memory
Painting bay
Frames on time, free of slag, spatter, burrs and sharp edges, labelled with the job number
Clean and check each frame before it leaves welding; agree hand-over times; warn them early of delays
Inspector (quality control)
Work already self-checked, marked, with the WPS and records kept with the job
Check your own work against the drawing first; accept findings without argument; ask what the drawing needs and put faults right quickly
Stores
Written requests with size, type and quantity, given early; signatures for what is drawn; unused rods and offcuts returned
Plan needs ahead and sign for stock, so it can be tracked and reordered before it runs out
Office (estimating and accounts)
Accurate hours and materials on every job card, handed in on time; any change the client asked for, reported at once
Hand in job cards on the agreed day; never leave a change unrecorded, or it will not be charged
Delivery driver
The size, mass and lifting points of each item, in writing, and the item ready at the agreed time
Write the details down so the right vehicle and lifting gear come
Other trades on a site
Work that fits the drawings and does not block their work
If there is a clash, check the drawing and agree the answer with the site lead, not trade to trade

blocks.note: The **job card** (also called a job sheet, work order or traveller) goes with a job through the shop. It lists the work, the materials, the checks and the hours. Keep it complete and honest: the office invoices from it, the stores reorder from it, and the next person learns from it what has been done.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: An **internal service agreement** is a short written list of what one section promises another. Each promise should be clear and measurable, so everyone can see whether it is kept.

head: From
To
Promise
How it is measured
rows: Welding
Painting bay
Frames passed on cleaned, deburred and labelled by 2 p.m. on the agreed day
Frames sent back for cleaning each week
Stores
Welding
Items on a written request issued within one working day
Percentage of requests met on time
Welding
Inspector
Every item self-checked against the drawing and marked before inspection
Percentage of items passed first time
Welding
Office
Complete job cards handed in every Friday by 3 p.m.
Number of job cards late each month

blocks.note: Agree each promise with the people it affects, keep the list short, put it up where everyone can see it, and review it at a short weekly meeting. When a promise keeps being broken, look for the cause instead of blaming people.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Finding out what the client needs

blocks.p: Clients often describe what they want loosely: 'a strong gate', 'something to stop thieves', 'a stand for the tank'. Your job is to turn that into an exact description that you can price and build, and that the client agrees with. Most arguments at handover start with a need that was never pinned down.

blocks.h: Questions that find the real need

head: Type of question
What it does
Examples
rows: Open
Gets the client talking about uses, wishes and worries; cannot be answered with yes or no
'What will the gate be used for?'
'Who will use the ramp, and how?'
'What worries you about the present grille?'
Probing (follow-up)
Gets more detail on something the client said
'You said trucks come in. How long are they?'
'How often is the hatch opened?'
Closed
Confirms one fact
'Is the opening 3.6 m wide?'
'Do you want it black?'
Summing up
Shows you understood and lets the client correct you
'So you need a sliding gate, 4.2 m wide, galvanised and painted black, fitted before 30 November. Have I got that right?'

blocks.p: Find out:

ul: What the item is for, and **who will use it**: children, older people, wheelchair users, vehicles, animals.
Sizes and the site: openings, levels, fixing surfaces, ground conditions.
Style, colour and finish; how secure it must be.
Any rule it must meet: rail height, gaps between bars, a way out in a fire.
The budget and the date it is needed.
Access for working and delivery; power on site (110 V or 220 V); when noise and sparks are allowed.
What is **not** part of the job: building work, electrical work for a gate motor, painting walls.
Face the client, let them finish, and take notes.
Do not plan your answer while they are still speaking.
Listen for the worry behind the words: cost, security, mess, a deadline such as a wedding or a school term.
Sum up what you heard and ask the client to correct you.

flow: Agree a time with the client
Ask your questions and record the answers on the client needs record
Measure everything yourself: widths at top, middle and bottom, heights, levels and diagonals
Note fixing surfaces, ground, access, power, hazards nearby and the setting, for example near the sea
Take photos with a tape in the shot
Draw a measured sketch
Send the sketch and notes to the client to confirm in writing
Prepare the quotation

blocks.note: Measure the site yourself rather than working from the client's figures. Openings are rarely square or level, and a client may measure brick to brick when the grille must fit inside a frame. A wrong size means remaking the work, a delay, and a cost the shop usually has to carry.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Send the client the sketch with the sizes and a note of what was agreed, and ask for confirmation by signature, email or a message you can keep. This protects both sides: a misunderstanding is caught before any steel is cut, not at handover.
Every client gets the same respect, time and honest prices, whatever their age, background, language, appearance, gender or disability.

ul: Speak in the way the client is comfortable with. Many Jamaicans are more at ease in Jamaican Creole; never talk down to anyone.

For a client who finds reading hard or has poor eyesight: go through the paperwork line by line, use sketches, offer large print, give time to decide, and ask the client to tell you back what they are agreeing to.

For a visitor with little English: use simple words, sketches, written numbers and photos of similar work; ask a colleague or someone the client trusts to translate, or use a phone translation tool for key points; then check understanding.

For a disabled client: speak to the client directly, not to the person with them, and ask how they will use the item, for example the height of a gate latch, the type of lock, or how a rail is gripped. Do not decide for them.
Confirm everything in writing for every client, and keep a copy.

blocks.note: Returning residents and clients abroad may give sizes in feet and inches. Convert to millimetres yourself (1 inch = 25.4 mm; 1 foot = 304.8 mm), write both on the sketch, and confirm the sizes on site.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Advising clients on materials, finishes and safe design

blocks.p: Clients rely on you to know what will last and what is safe. Good advice sets out the choices, the reasons and the cost of each, in plain words, then lets the client decide. Never run down a choice just to make a bigger sale, and never agree to build something you know is unsafe.

head: Finish
How it protects
Good points
Points to explain
rows: Painted mild steel
The paint keeps air, water and salt off the steel
Lowest first cost; any colour
Chips and scratches let rust start
Near the sea it needs repainting often
Welds must be cleaned of slag and spatter first, or rust starts there
Hot-dip galvanised (HDG)
The finished item is dipped in a bath of melted zinc, which coats every surface, inside and out
Lasts much longer; the zinc goes on protecting the steel even at a scratch, because the zinc corrodes first
Costs more
Adds the galvaniser's time, often about a week
Hollow parts need vent and drain holes
Welding it afterwards gives off zinc fume and burns off the coat
Galvanised and painted (duplex)
Zinc under paint
Longest life of the steel finishes near the sea; any colour
Costs most of the steel finishes
The paint needs the primer the paint maker names for galvanised steel
Stainless steel
Chromium in the steel forms a thin protective film; no coating to chip
Bright, hygienic, little upkeep
Highest cost
Needs the right grade: 316 is usually advised near the sea or a pool, 304 for most indoor and kitchen work
Still needs washing near salt to avoid brown staining
Needs a welder skilled in stainless

ul: **Marine (coastal) environment:** salt carried in the air from the sea settles on steel and makes it rust much faster. Much of Jamaica's population and most hotels are on or near the coast. Advise galvanising, a duplex finish or stainless steel, and washing with fresh water from time to time.
**Pools:** chlorine and salt spray attack steel; even stainless steel needs the right grade.
**Food areas:** worktables, sinks and shelves that touch food should be **food-grade stainless steel**. It does not rust, has no coating to chip into food, and is easy to clean and sanitise.
**Sheltered, dry, inland:** a good paint system on mild steel may be enough, if the client accepts that it will need some upkeep.

blocks.note: Explain in the client's terms, not yours. For example: 'Painted steel costs least today, but this close to the sea the paint will chip and the steel will rust within a few years. Galvanising costs more and adds about a week, but the zinc keeps protecting the steel even where it gets scratched, so it lasts many years longer. If you want colour, we can paint over the zinc.' Then give the price and upkeep of each choice and let the client decide.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Request
What to advise
Why
rows: A tank stand 'as cheap as possible'
Explain the load and quote the sizes that are safe
Each litre of water has a mass of about 1 kg, so a full 2 000-litre tank weighs about 2 tonnes, plus the tank. A weak stand can collapse on people.
Burglar bars fixed shut over every bedroom window
At least one escape grille in each bedroom that opens quickly from inside, with the key kept close by
People are trapped behind fixed grilles in house fires
Railings where small children play
Vertical bars, with the height and gaps the building rules or the standard require
Children climb horizontal bars and can slip through wide gaps
A heavy vehicle gate
Hinges, posts, wheels and stops sized for the gate's weight and the slope of the drive
A heavy gate on light fittings sags, drags and can fall
Hollow sections to be galvanised
Vent and drain holes in the places the galvaniser advises
Air or moisture trapped in a closed section can burst it in the hot zinc bath

blocks.note: Fire officers in Jamaica regularly warn that fixed burglar bars trap people in house fires. When you fit grilles to a home, show the family how to open the escape grille and agree where the key will hang.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **quotation** is a written offer: this work, to this standard, for this price, by this time. A clear quotation prevents most arguments later.

head: Part of the quotation
What it says
rows: Client and reference
Name, address and phone; the shop's reference number; the date
The work
What will be made and fitted, with sizes and the sketch or drawing reference
Material and finish
For example 40 × 40 × 3 mm square tube, hot-dip galvanised, then painted black, with a short reason for the advice
Exclusions
What is not included, for example masonry, electrical work for a gate motor, painting of walls
Price
In J$, broken down where it helps the client (materials, labour, galvanising, fitting)
GCT
On its own line, 'at the current rate'; or the words 'prices exclude GCT', which mean GCT will be added on top
Deposit and payment terms
For example a 50% deposit before work starts, the balance on completion
Lead time
The time to finish, in working days from the deposit, including outside work such as galvanising
Validity
How long the price holds; steel prices change
Warranty
What the shop will put right free, and for how long
Signatures
The person who prepared it, and the client's acceptance

blocks.note: **GCT** (General Consumption Tax) is added to most goods and services in Jamaica. The Government sets the rate and can change it, so quotations say 'GCT at the current rate' and the invoice uses the rate on the day it is made. Never quote a GCT figure from memory.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Sums you must be able to do

ul: **A percentage of an amount:** amount × percentage ÷ 100.
**What percentage one amount is of another:** part ÷ whole × 100.
**Percentage overrun:** (actual − promised) ÷ promised × 100.

head: Question
Working
Answer
rows: A 40% deposit on a J$185 000 grille job
The balance after that deposit, before GCT
A client has paid J$45 000 on a J$150 000 job. What percentage is that?
Promised in 12 working days, ready on day 15. By what percentage was it late?
A deposit of J$63 000 was 35% of the price. What was the full price?

blocks.note: Check every sum a second way before it goes on paper. For example, a 40% deposit must be a little less than half the price: J$74 000 is a little less than half of J$185 000, so it is sensible.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Document
What it is for
rows: Quotation
The offer: work, price, time and terms
Variation (change) order
A written, agreed change to the work, the price or the time, signed before the change is made
Delivery note
Signed by the client when goods are handed over; proof that the shop delivered them
Invoice
The bill: what is owed, with GCT on its own line
Receipt
Proof that a payment was made
Warranty
The shop's written promise to put right its own faulty work free of charge for a stated period
Care notes and test or inspection records
How to look after the item; proof that it was checked

blocks.p: When a client cannot see why a job costs what it does or takes as long as it does, walk them through the steps: for a trailer repair, for example, strip the damaged part, cut out the crack, weld, check the weld, prime and paint, and let the paint dry. A client who understands the work is far less likely to argue about the bill.

sections.title: Managing expectations: dates, delays and changes

blocks.p: Clients judge you on whether you did what you said, when you said. Promise what you can deliver, then deliver it, or tell the client early.
The **lead time** is the time from the order (usually the deposit) to the finished job. Add up every step, including work done outside the shop.

head: Step
Working days
rows: Steel delivered from the supplier
Make in the shop
At the galvaniser
Paint and let it dry
Fit on site
Lead time to give the client
14 working days, plus a little extra if the weather or a supplier is uncertain

blocks.note: Say 'working days' and count them on a calendar. Allow for public holidays (for example Labour Day in May, and Emancipation Day and Independence Day close together in August), the galvaniser's closing days and the shop's own shutdown. '14 working days from your deposit' is clearer than 'about two weeks'.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: When a job will be late

flow: Find out the real new date: ask the supplier, and check whether another source can help at a fair price
Re-plan: do now whatever can be done (templates, fixings, paint ready) to save time later
Call the client before the due date: apologise, give the real reason, and a new date you are sure of
If the delay hurts the client, offer help, such as a temporary way to secure a doorway
Confirm the new date in writing, and update the client if anything changes again

blocks.p: A client who hears bad news early can plan, and usually understands. A client who finds out on the day feels let down, may not come back, and tells others.

ul: Do not make the change on the spot, and do not refuse it out of hand.
Write down exactly what the client wants.
Work out the effect on the price, the time, the materials and any work already done.
Agree it in writing on a **variation order**, signed before the work changes.
Update the drawing, the job card and the team. Never bill a change the client did not agree to.
Agree working times, noise, and where sparks and fumes will go, especially at a shop, school, hotel or office that stays open.
Put up barriers and screens; protect floors, goods and vehicles from sparks and spatter.
Keep clients, staff, children and passers-by away from the arc. If someone comes to watch, stop and screen the work.
Keep the client's property secure while you work: close gates you opened, and do not leave a building open.
Tidy daily, and leave the site swept: offcuts and rod stubs can cut, burn or trip people, and a clean site shows care.

blocks.p: Missed dates are usually a planning problem, not a welding problem. Keep the shop's jobs on a planning board with promised dates, check progress each morning, order steel and book the galvaniser early, and give dates from the board, not from hope.

sections.title: Unsafe and unwise requests, honesty and confidentiality

blocks.p: Sometimes a client asks for something that would put people at risk, or asks you to say something that is not true. Pleasing the client stops here. Your aim is to keep everyone safe and still leave the client feeling well served.

flow: Thank the client and listen to what they are trying to achieve
Explain the danger calmly, in plain words
Offer safe choices, with the price and time for each
Let the client choose
If they insist on the unsafe way, refuse politely and firmly
Record the request and tell your supervisor

head: Request
The danger
What to do
rows: Cut or weld a drum, tank or container that held fuel, oil or chemicals
Vapour left inside can explode, even when the container looks empty
No hot work until a competent person has cleaned it and proved it gas-free under the shop's hot work procedure; or cut it cold after cleaning; or make the item from new steel
Weld a crack in a cooking-gas (LPG) cylinder
A gas cylinder is a pressure vessel: a welded repair can burst
Refuse; the cylinder goes out of use and back to the gas supplier
Weld a patch on a vehicle's fuel tank while it is fitted
Fuel and vapour in and around the tank can catch fire or explode
No hot work in place; the tank is removed, emptied and made safe by a competent person, or replaced
Weld a crack in a forklift fork, lifting hook, chain or shackle
Welding changes the steel; lifting equipment can then fail suddenly under load
Take it out of use; refer it to the maker or a lifting-equipment inspector; replace it
Weld a cracked wheel rim with the tyre still fitted
Heat can make the tyre burst; a welded rim can crack again on the road
Refuse; the wheel is replaced
Fix burglar bars shut over every window
People can be trapped in a fire
Advise an escape grille in each bedroom
Sign that an item is 'inspected' or 'certified' when you only did part of the work
A false statement; people may rely on it with their lives
Decline; write and sign only for the work you actually did

blocks.note: Never do hot work on a closed container, a vehicle's fuel system or lifting equipment because a client is in a hurry or is a good customer. Welders have been killed by 'empty' drums. If you are unsure, stop and ask your supervisor.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Charge only for work done and materials used, and record them truthfully on the job card.
Do not promise a date you know you cannot meet.
Own up to the shop's mistakes and put them right.
Sign only for what you did or saw yourself.
Use clients' names, addresses, phone numbers and prices only for their job. Jamaica's data protection law requires businesses to protect people's personal information.
Keep drawings of security grilles, strong-room doors and safes private, and give them only to the client or people the client names: in the wrong hands they show how to break in.
Do not discuss one client's job or price with another client.
Do not post photos of a client's home or security work online without the client's permission.

blocks.p: Using the shop's machines, materials or time for private jobs, or taking the shop's clients for yourself, takes work and money from the business that employs you. It is a breach of trust and usually of your terms of employment. If a client asks you to do a job 'on the side', refer them to the shop.

flow: Stay calm and let the client finish: do not interrupt, argue or raise your voice
Apologise for the trouble; this is not yet admitting fault
Record it on the complaint log: who, what, when, job number
Agree when you will inspect, and do it soon
Inspect with the client and find the cause
Explain what you found in plain words
Agree the repair and the date, and apply the warranty fairly
Do the repair and check it with the client
Call a few days later to check all is well
Find the root cause and change the shop's method

head: With an angry client, do
Avoid
rows: Listen fully and let them finish
Interrupting, arguing or matching their tone
Use their name; keep your voice low and steady
Blaming the client, a co-worker or another section in front of them
Move to a quieter place, away from other clients
Walking away, or leaving them waiting with no news
Say exactly what you will do, and by when
Promising what you cannot authorise, such as a refund

blocks.note: If the complaint is about something you do not handle, such as a billing error, do not brush it off with 'not my department', and do not promise what only someone else can give. Take the details, pass them on at once to the person who handles it, and tell the client who will contact them and by when.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Putting one gate right satisfies one client. Finding why it went wrong, and changing the shop's method, protects every client after.

head: Complaint
Possible root cause
Change in the shop
rows: Rust spots at the welds a few months after fitting
Slag and spatter not removed before painting; sharp edges left, where paint is thin
A cleaning and edge check before painting, signed on the job card
Swing gate sags or drags
Hinge weld too small or cracked; post not set firmly; hinges too light for the gate
Size hinges and posts for the gate; check the swing at handover
Sliding gate jumps its track
Track not level or not straight; guide rollers loose; no end stops
Check the track level and guides at fitting; fit end stops; give care notes on keeping the track clear
Grille does not fit the opening
Client's own sizes used
Always measure on site
Sharp edges and burrs
Finishing step skipped
Add an edge check to the inspection sheet

blocks.p: A **warranty** (or guarantee) is the shop's written promise, usually given with the invoice, to put right its own faulty work free of charge for a stated period, for example 6 or 12 months on workmanship. It covers faults in the shop's work under normal use; it does not usually cover accidents, misuse or changes made by others. When a fault in your work shows within the period, repair it free and find out why it happened. Fair handling of warranty claims keeps clients loyal.

flow: Check the work against the drawing and the snag list, and put right what is wrong
Clean the site: offcuts, rod stubs, spatter and packaging removed
Walk round with the client and show what was done, including any agreed changes
Show how to use, lock and look after the item
Explain any limits: the load it was made for, no extra tanks, no later cutting or welding without advice
Hand over the papers and get the delivery note signed

head: Papers for the client
Why
rows: Invoice
What is owed, with GCT shown
Warranty terms
What is covered and for how long
Test or inspection records, if any
Proof that the work was checked
Care notes
For example: wash off salt and dust, touch up chips quickly, oil hinges and rollers, keep tracks clear
The shop's contact details
So the client knows whom to call
Delivery note (the client signs; the shop keeps it)
Proof of handover

ul: Call the client a few days after fitting a large item, to check that it works and to catch small snags early.
Keep a **job record** for every job: date, the fault found or the work asked for, the work done, the materials used and who did it. When the client calls again, you can answer at once.
Treat each call-back as a chance to keep the client for the next job.

blocks.p: A **service standard** is a clear, measurable promise about service, such as how fast messages are returned or how many jobs are ready on the promised date. Standards turn 'good service' into something the team can see, measure and improve.

head: Area
Example standard
How it is measured
rows: Messages
Every message returned the same working day
Message log
Quotations
Written quotation within 2 working days of the site visit
Visit date and quotation date in the log
Dates
At least 9 jobs in 10 ready by the promised date
Promised and actual dates on the job cards
Complaints
Every complaint answered within 1 working day; site visit within 3
Complaint log
Getting it right first time
Fewer than 1 job in 20 needs a return visit to fix the shop's work
Return-visit log

ul: Agree them with the team, so they are realistic.
Write them down and put them where staff can see them.
Make each one measurable: a number, a time or a percentage.
Keep simple records so each one can be checked.
Review them regularly, and raise them as the shop improves.

head: Result
Working
Score
rows: 47 of 50 jobs ready on time
6 return visits in 40 jobs
15%, about 1 job in 7
33 of 36 clients said they would use the shop again
about 92%

blocks.p: A figure on its own changes nothing. Compare it with the standard, find the cause of any shortfall (late steel, poor planning, skipped checks), fix it, and share the results with the team. Many return visits, for example, usually mean the checks before handover need improving.

blocks.note: Be exact about time. '48 hours' from a site visit at 2 p.m. on Monday ends at 2 p.m. on Wednesday. '2 working days' from Monday ends at the close of work on Wednesday. Say which you mean, in the standard and to the client.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say 'I can' to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain the difference between internal and external customers, with examples from a fabrication shop.
I can say what the painting bay, the inspector, the stores, the office and the driver need from the welding team, and how to serve them well.
I can write clear, measurable promises for an internal service agreement.
I can use open, probing, closed and summing-up questions to find out what a client needs.
I can plan and carry out a site visit, measure the site myself and confirm the needs in writing.
I can serve every client fairly, including clients with a disability, older clients and clients who speak another language.
I can explain painted, galvanised, duplex and stainless finishes in plain words and help a client choose.
I can give safe design advice on tank stands, burglar bars, railings, gates and hollow sections.
I can list what a quotation must contain, and show GCT 'at the current rate'.
I can work out deposits, balances, percentages, overruns and lead times.
I can tell a client about a delay early and agree a change on a variation order before doing it.
I can refuse an unsafe request politely, explain why, and offer safe choices.
I can keep clients' details and security drawings confidential, and act honestly.
I can handle a complaint from the first call to the follow-up, and find its root cause.
I can hand over a job with the right checks, explanations and papers.
I can set service standards, measure them, and act on the results.

terms: Client needs record
A form for writing down what the client asked for and agreed at the enquiry or site visit
Complaint log
A record of each complaint, when it came in, and what was done about it
Delivery note
A document the client signs when goods are handed over; proof of delivery
Deposit
A part payment made before work starts, to secure the order and pay for materials
Duplex finish
Hot-dip galvanising with paint on top
Exclusions
Things a quotation states are not part of the job
External customer
A person or business outside the shop who buys its goods or services
Food-grade stainless steel
Stainless steel suitable for surfaces that touch food
GCT
General Consumption Tax, added on top of most prices at the rate the Government sets
Hot-dip galvanised (HDG)
Coated by dipping in a bath of melted zinc
Internal customer
A person or section in the same business who depends on your team's work
Internal service agreement
A short written list of measurable promises one section makes to another
Invoice
The bill, showing what is owed and the GCT
Job card
The card or sheet that travels with a job, listing the work, materials, checks and hours; also called a job sheet, work order or traveller
Lead time
The time from the order to the finished job
Marine (coastal) environment
A setting near the sea, where salt in the air makes steel rust faster
Open question
A question that cannot be answered with yes or no, so the client explains
Quality control (QC)
Checking work against the drawing and standard before it goes to the client
Quotation
A written offer giving the work, price, time and terms
Root cause
The basic reason something went wrong, which, if fixed, stops it happening again
Service standard
A clear, measurable promise about service
Snag list
A list of small faults to put right before handover
Variation order
A written, agreed change to the work, price or time
Warranty
The shop's written promise to put right its own faulty work free for a stated period; also called a guarantee

c1.title: A ramp handrail for a church in Old Harbour Bay
c1.text: Pastor Errol Grant of a church in Old Harbour Bay, St Catherine, phones Dwight Campbell, the Level 3 welder who leads the site team at a fabrication shop in Spanish Town. The church is about 200 metres from the sea. The pastor wants 'a rail for the new ramp, something nice and not too dear'. Several older members walk with sticks, and Sister Marcia uses a wheelchair. The pastor measured the ramp himself and says it is '9 metres or so'.

c2.title: The week before Christmas in the Spanish Town shop
c2.text: It is the busiest week of the year at the Spanish Town shop, and Dwight is running the welding team. Nadine in the painting bay says three frames reached her with spatter and sharp edges, and one had no job number. Mr Wint in the stores says electrodes ran out twice because welders took packets without signing for them. The office says the welding team's job cards are coming in days late, and several clients have not yet been invoiced.

c3.title: Three requests at a haulage yard near Junction
c3.text: Mr Lindo runs a small haulage and farm-supply business near Junction, St Elizabeth, and is one of the shop's best clients. While Shernette, a Level 3 welder, is fitting a new ramp at his yard, he asks her to weld a crack in one of his forklift forks 'just to get through the week', and to weld a patch on a leaking diesel tank that is still fitted to his truck. He says he is in a hurry and will pay cash.

c4.title: A sliding gate in Portmore
c4.text: Ten weeks ago the shop made and fitted a sliding gate for Mrs Simone Rowe in Portmore, St Catherine. The shop's written warranty covers its workmanship for 12 months. Mrs Rowe phones Dwight, very angry: the gate has jumped off its track twice, and it nearly hit her car. When Dwight visits, he finds that the track was fixed with a slope along its length and that no end stop was fitted at the open end.

c5.title: Canteen grilles for a school in Morant Bay
c5.text: A high school in Morant Bay, St Thomas, ordered galvanised grilles for its canteen windows. The school paid a 40% deposit of J$128 000, and the quotation promised fitting 15 working days after the deposit. On the eighth working day, the galvaniser tells Dwight that its zinc bath will be shut for repairs for a week. The same afternoon, the principal, Mrs Hamilton, asks for a lockable serving hatch to be added to one of the grilles.

questions.q: What should Dwight do before he gives the pastor a price?
o: Price 9 m of rail from the pastor's figure, adding 10% to be safe
Send two prices, one for the cheapest rail and one for the best
Visit the church, ask how the ramp is used and measure it himself
Ask the pastor to send a photo of the ramp to price it from
questions.why: A price is only as good as the information behind it. Seeing the ramp, hearing how members use it and measuring it himself lets Dwight price the right rail; a rough length and a photo hide slopes, fixings and the users' needs.

questions.q: On the visit, which of Dwight's questions is an open question that will tell him most about what the rail must do?
o: Who uses the ramp, and how do they use it?
Is the ramp exactly 9 metres long?
Would you like the rail painted black?
Do you want a rail on both sides of the ramp?
questions.why: An open question cannot be answered with yes or no, so the pastor has to describe the users and how they move. That tells Dwight about grip, height, and rails on one or both sides. The others are closed questions that confirm single facts.

questions.q: The pastor asks why Dwight advises galvanising the rail before it is painted, when paint alone is cheaper. Which explanation is right?
o: Paint alone is fine for a few years, but then it gets dull and needs a fresh coat
Galvanised tube is stronger, so a smaller tube can be used for the rail
Salt air this near the sea soon rusts steel wherever the paint chips
Paint will not stick to new steel unless it has been galvanised first
questions.why: Near the sea, salt in the air rusts steel quickly wherever paint is chipped or thin. The zinc coat goes on protecting the steel even at a scratch, so the rail lasts far longer. Galvanising does not make steel stronger.

questions.q: Sister Marcia, who uses a wheelchair, comes to the site visit with her daughter. How should Dwight involve her?
o: Ask her daughter how her mother uses the ramp, to save her any trouble
Ask Sister Marcia herself how she uses the ramp and grips the rail
Leave her out of it, since the pastor is the one placing the order
Design the rail to the pastor's wishes, then ask her if she likes it
questions.why: Speak to a disabled client directly, not through the person with her. She knows best how she moves up the ramp and what she can grip, and her answers set the rail height and shape.

questions.q: After the visit, how should Dwight confirm what the pastor needs?
o: Rely on the notes he took, as he wrote everything down at the visit
Phone the pastor and read all his notes to him before the order is placed
Give the sizes to the fitters now so they can start cutting early
Send a sketch with sizes and notes, and ask for confirmation in writing
questions.why: A written confirmation of a sketch catches any misunderstanding before steel is cut, and it protects both the church and the shop if there is a dispute at handover.

questions.q: In this story, who are the welding team's internal customers?
o: The clients who are still waiting for their frames to be finished and fitted
Only Nadine, because she is the one who receives the frames
Nadine, Mr Wint and the office, who all need something from the team
The clients and the steel supplier, who both deal with the shop
questions.why: Internal customers work in the same business and depend on the team: the painting bay needs clean frames, the stores need signatures to reorder, and the office needs job cards to invoice. Clients and suppliers are outside the business.

questions.q: Dwight and Nadine agree to write down one promise from welding to the painting bay. Which is written best?
o: Welders will do their very best to keep all frames as clean as they possibly can
The painting bay will get good, clean frames in good time from the welders from now on
Frames reach painting cleaned, deburred and labelled by 2 p.m. on the agreed day
Welding will tell the painting bay whenever a batch of frames is ready to come over
questions.why: A useful promise is clear and measurable: anyone can check whether a frame arrived clean, deburred, labelled and on time. 'Do their best' and 'good frames' cannot be measured, so nobody knows whether they were kept.

questions.q: What is the main harm to the business from the late job cards?
o: The welders' hours cannot be counted for their overtime pay
Work goes uninvoiced, so the shop is paid late or not at all
The inspector cannot tell which welder made each frame
The painting bay does not know which colour each frame needs
questions.why: The office invoices from the hours and materials on the job card. Late or incomplete cards mean late invoices, slow payment and changes that are never charged. The team leader should agree a fixed day for handing them in.

questions.q: Which reply to the request about the forklift fork is right?
o: Weld it with low-hydrogen electrodes, then grind it smooth
Weld it, but tell him to lift only half loads until a new one comes
Weld a steel plate over the crack to make the fork even stronger
Take it out of use; the maker or an inspector decides on a new fork
questions.why: Lifting equipment must not be repaired by welding on site: the heat changes the steel, and the fork can snap under load with someone nearby. It goes out of use until the maker or a lifting-equipment inspector decides.

questions.q: Why must Shernette not weld the patch on the diesel tank while it is fitted to the truck?
o: Diesel is hard to set alight, so the only real risk is a smoky weld
Fuel and vapour in and around the tank can catch fire or explode
Diesel tanks are made from a metal that cannot be welded at all
The welding would leave a mark that spoils the truck's paint
questions.why: Any tank that holds fuel can contain vapour that explodes when heated, and fuel near the weld can catch fire. The tank must be removed, emptied and made safe by a competent person, or replaced.

questions.q: Mr Lindo is annoyed when Shernette says no. How can she refuse and still serve him well?
o: Do just the fork as a favour, since he is one of the best clients
Explain the dangers, offer safe options with prices, and record it
Refuse both jobs, then finish the ramp quickly and leave the yard at once
Tell him that the shop's rules are to blame, not her own decision
questions.why: Saying why, in plain words, and offering safe ways to meet the need (a new fork, a tank removed and made safe, or a new tank) keeps him safe and keeps him as a client. Recording the request protects her and the shop.

questions.q: When Mrs Rowe phones, angry, what should Dwight do first?
o: Explain that sliding gates jump if their owners do not keep them clean
Tell her a welder will come today and fix it, whatever the cause
Ask her to call back later, when she is calm enough to talk it through
Let her finish, apologise for the trouble, and write down the details
questions.why: An angry client first needs to be heard. Letting her finish, apologising for the trouble and recording the facts calms the call and gives Dwight what he needs. Blaming her, or promising a fix before knowing the cause, makes things worse.

questions.q: Mrs Rowe asks whether she will have to pay for the repair. What is the fair answer, given what Dwight found?
o: Yes, because gates need servicing by the owner after a few weeks
She pays for the visit, but the repair itself will cost her nothing
Only half, as the warranty covers half the cost after two months
No: the fault is in the shop's fitting, so the warranty covers it
questions.why: A sloping track and a missing end stop are faults in the shop's own work, found within the 12-month warranty, so the repair is free. A warranty covers faults in workmanship under normal use, not misuse or damage.

questions.q: What should the shop change so that this does not happen on the next sliding gate?
o: Add a track level and end-stop check to the fitting and handover sheet
Tell the fitters to take more care with tracks on every job from now on
Stop making sliding gates and offer clients swing gates instead
Give clients a discount in future instead of making return visits
questions.why: The root cause was a skipped check, so the fix is a check that cannot be skipped: written on the sheet and signed. 'Take more care' changes nothing that can be checked, and avoiding sliding gates does not solve the fault.

questions.q: After the repair, Mrs Rowe asks how she can help the gate run well. Which care advice is right?
o: Oil the track heavily every week so that the wheels slide over it easily
Keep the track clear of stones and dirt, and have the rollers checked
Push the gate firmly so that it rides over any dirt on the track
Paint the track every month so that it cannot start to rust
questions.why: Stones and dirt on the track lift the wheel and can make the gate jump; worn or loose rollers do the same. Heavy oil collects grit, and paint on the running surface soon wears off.

questions.q: When the galvaniser's news comes in, what is Dwight's best first step?
o: Find out the real reopening date and whether another galvaniser can help
Wait a few days in case the galvaniser manages to reopen the bath sooner
Paint the grilles instead of galvanising them, so the date is still kept
Say nothing until the due date, then explain to the school what went wrong
questions.why: Dwight needs the facts before he calls the school: the real date, and whether another galvaniser could do the work. Then he can tell Mrs Hamilton promptly, with an honest reason and a new date he can keep. Changing the finish without her agreement breaks the order.

questions.q: Mrs Hamilton agrees to the price and extra time for the serving hatch. Which document should record the change before work on it starts?
o: A new delivery note, signed when the hatch is fitted
A note on the job card that only the welders see
A variation order, signed by the school and the shop
A second deposit receipt for the extra amount paid
questions.why: A variation order records the agreed change to the work, the price and the time, signed before the change is made, so there is no dispute at the end. The job card and the team are then updated from it.

questions.q: The school's deposit of J$128 000 was 40% of the price. What was the full price, before GCT?
questions.why: If 40% is J$128 000, then 1% is J$3 200 and 100% is J$320 000. J$192 000 is the balance still to pay; J$179 200 wrongly adds 40% to the deposit.

questions.q: A shop's standard is that at least 9 jobs in 10 are ready on the promised date. In October, 41 of 48 jobs were on time. What should the team leader conclude?
o: At about 94%, the shop beat its standard comfortably
At about 85%, the shop has met its standard for the month
At about 85%, the standard was missed; find the causes
Nothing can be judged until the end of the year
questions.why: 41 ÷ 48 × 100 is about 85%, below the 90% the standard asks for. The team leader should look for the causes, such as late steel or poor planning, and fix them.

questions.q: A man says he is a client's brother and asks for a copy of the drawing of her new strong-room door, 'to check the quality'. What should you do?
o: Give him a copy, as he is family and wants to help his sister
Show him the drawing in the office, but do not let him keep a copy
Politely refuse, and tell him to ask the client to contact you
Send it to him by phone message, so that there is a record
questions.why: Drawings of security work show how to get past it, so they go only to the client or people she names. Refusing politely and referring him to the client protects her without being rude to him.
